aboutKids: A friendly dog says bow wow, and someone asks who he belongs to. He is little Tom Tinker's dog!
story: This tiny dog rhyme is anonymous. It was printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, one of the first English nursery-rhyme books, under the title Caesar's Song. Later collections, including 19th-century American picture books, kept it alive, sometimes renaming the owner Tom Tucker. Little Duet sets the words to its own simple chant.
funFact: In one of the very first nursery-rhyme books, printed around 1765, this little dog rhyme appeared under the title Caesar's Song.
catalogNote: Catalog dates the words to Halliwell (1842), but the rhyme was already printed c. 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody as 'Caesar's Song' (Opie, Oxford Dictionary of Nursery Rhymes no. 138, per Representative Poetry Online). Suggest updating origin and publicDomainBasis to c. 1765; public-domain status is unaffected.

aboutKids: Quick, quick! Jack is a speedy, bouncy boy who jumps right over a candlestick in one big leap.
story: An anonymous English rhyme, first found handwritten in a manuscript of about 1815 and printed by James Orchard Halliwell in 1844. It may echo an old custom of jumping over candlesticks, both as a sport and as a way of telling fortunes. It is usually chanted rather than sung.
funFact: Children have long used it as a jump-rope rhyme, which is why it is more often chanted than sung.
catalogNote: Catalog says the rhyme was printed c. 1798 (Harley manuscript). The sources found (Opie via the Traditional Ballad Index; Wikipedia) give the earliest record as a manuscript of c. 1815 (Douce MS), first printed by Halliwell in 1844. No evidence found for a c. 1798 Harley manuscript. Public-domain status is unaffected.

aboutKids: It is raining, and a little one wants to go outside and play, so they kindly ask the rain to go away.
story: Children have chanted rain charms for centuries. James Howell's 1659 proverb collection has an early version sending the rain to Spain, and John Aubrey (1687) noted children asking it to return another day. The familiar wording, with a child who wants to play, appears in Halliwell's 1844 collection. It is sung to the playground sol-mi-la chant.
funFact: Older versions told the rain to go away to Spain, or asked it to come back again on Saturday instead.
myth: Sometimes said to be about the Spanish Armada of 1588. No evidence links it to the Armada; the earliest record (1659) is simply a weather charm, and similar rain rhymes exist in many cultures.
catalogNote: Catalog credits the first record to John Aubrey (1687). An earlier version appears in James Howell's proverbs (1659); Aubrey's is a different variant, and the modern 'go away' wording dates from the 19th century (Halliwell, 1844). Public-domain status is unaffected.

aboutKids: Up and down, up and down! Margery goes for a ride on a seesaw, rocking high and then low.
story: An anonymous rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, a London collection. It may have begun as a work chant for pairs of sawyers pulling a long saw back and forth, and later became a seesaw game. No real Margery Daw is known; the name probably just rhymes.
funFact: A London play from 1640 already linked a see-saw chant to workers sawing wood together, more than a century before this rhyme was printed.

aboutKids: When the very first star twinkles in the evening sky, you make a quiet wish and hope it comes true.
story: An anonymous American wishing rhyme, first written down in the 1860s and 1870s, when it was linked to fortune-telling. The custom of wishing on the first star of the evening may be older than the rhyme itself. It reached Britain by the early 20th century and is usually spoken, not sung.
funFact: Families traditionally say it the moment they spot the first star of the evening, and then make a wish.
catalogNote: Catalog says 'late 19th century'. The earliest cited printing is 1866 (William Furniss), so 'mid-to-late 19th century' is more precise. Public-domain status is unaffected.

writtenBy: Traditional English song; c. 1780 sheet music attributed to William Swords
aboutKids: A farmer has a happy dog named Bingo, and everyone spells his name together, clapping in place of letters.
story: The earliest trace is sheet music from about 1780 credited to William Swords, an actor at London's Haymarket Theatre, with the dog then often called little Bingo. It was reprinted in 1785, noted in the United States by 1842, and grew into a spelling and clapping game for children.
funFact: In some places the dog had other names, like Bango or Pinto, and sometimes his owner was a miller or a shepherd.
catalogNote: Catalog cites a c. 1780 version titled 'Bob Bingo'. Sources found date the earliest reference to c. 1780 sheet music attributed to William Swords, but do not confirm the title 'Bob Bingo' (early names are 'Bingo' or 'Little Bingo'). US presence is noted from 1842; the claim of the modern form in 1880s US collections was not confirmed. Public-domain status is unaffected.

aboutKids: A grown-up softly sings to a sleepy baby, promising one lovely present after another, like a singing mockingbird and a shiny ring.
story: A lullaby from the Southern United States with no known author. The English collector Cecil Sharp wrote down a version in Franklin County, Virginia, in 1918, the earliest on record. Its chain of promised gifts follows an old swapping-song pattern. Folk singers such as Jean Ritchie, Burl Ives and Joan Baez spread it widely.
funFact: The earliest written version dates from 1918, when a visiting English song collector heard it sung in Virginia.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: James William Elliott
aboutKids: Jack and Jill climb up a hill to fetch a pail of water, then take a big tumble all the way down.
story: An anonymous rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, where the girl's name was spelled Gill. Jack and Jill was already an everyday English phrase for any boy and girl. The tune most families sing was published by James William Elliott in National Nursery Rhymes and Nursery Songs (1870).
funFact: In the earliest printed version, more than 250 years ago, Jill's name was spelled Gill.
myth: Claimed to hide stories about a Norse moon legend, a tax on drink measures under Charles I, Tudor politicians, or a couple from a Somerset village. These ideas mostly appeared after the rhyme was printed and have no supporting evidence.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme and singing game
aboutKids: Two children make a bridge with their arms, everyone sings that it is falling down, and the bridge gently catches a friend.
story: A singing game of unknown authorship. Dancing the building of London Bridge is mentioned in a play written around 1636, and the words were printed in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book around 1744. The tune families know today was first printed in 1879, in A. H. Rosewig's American collection of songs and games.
funFact: A real London Bridge, built in 1831, was taken apart stone by stone and rebuilt in Lake Havasu City, Arizona.
myth: Often said to recall a Viking attack on the bridge in 1014, or a legend of a person sealed into its foundations. The Viking 'evidence' is an 1844 translation shaped by the rhyme itself, and neither theory is proven.

aboutKids: Old MacDonald has a busy farm full of animals, and each one makes its own noisy sound, from moo to oink to quack.
story: A folk song of unknown authorship. A similar farmyard song appears in Thomas d'Urfey's opera of 1706, and English collectors found versions in the 1900s. An early printing called Ohio, with a farmer named Old Macdougal, appeared in Tommy's Tunes (1917), a book of First World War songs. Recordings in the 1920s settled the familiar name and tune.
funFact: The farmer was not always MacDonald. A 1917 version called him Old Macdougal, and his famous name only settled in during the 1920s.

aboutKids: Clap, clap! We help the baker make a cake, pat it, mark it with a letter, and pop it in the oven.
story: This clapping rhyme first appears in Thomas D'Urfey's play The Campaigners (1698), recited by a nurse to the children in her care, and it was probably older still. A different wording was printed in Mother Goose's Melody around 1765, and James Hook set it to music in 1796. Little Duet uses its own sol-mi-la chant.
funFact: Grown-ups have played this clapping game with little ones for over 300 years, often swapping in the child's own initial.

year: 1881 (words first printed in English); melody reported c. 1790
origin: England and the United States, with European relatives
aboutKids: Friends hold hands, skip around in a circle, and then everyone falls down together with a giggle.
story: An anonymous ring game. A related rhyme was printed in Germany in 1796 and versions were noted in the US in the 1840s. The familiar English words appeared in Kate Greenaway's Mother Goose (1881) and William Wells Newell's Games and Songs of American Children (1883). Many early versions had no falling down at all.
funFact: In many old versions, players ended with a curtsy or a bow instead of tumbling to the ground.
myth: Widely said to describe the Great Plague of 1665 or the Black Death. Folklorists reject this: the plague reading only appeared in the mid-20th century, and the earliest versions lack the sneezing and falling it relies on.

writtenBy: Words: unknown, published by Charles Bradlee. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman'
aboutKids: We sing every letter from A all the way to Z, so we can learn our ABCs together.
story: The Boston music publisher Charles Bradlee copyrighted the song in 1835 as The A.B.C., a German air with variations for the flute. Who wrote the words is unknown. The melody is the French tune also used for Twinkle Twinkle Little Star, first printed in 1761.
funFact: The same tune helps children learn their alphabets in many languages, including Spanish, German, French, Japanese and Korean.
myth: Often said that Mozart composed the tune. He wrote twelve piano variations on it around 1781-82, but the melody had already been printed in France in 1761.
catalogNote: Catalog presents Bradlee as the source; he was the publisher who copyrighted the song, and the lyricist is unknown. His edition called the tune a 'German air' and credited Louis Le Maire, though the melody is the French 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman'. Public-domain status is unaffected.

writtenBy: Words: Jane Taylor. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman' (composer unknown)
aboutKids: A child looks up at a tiny, sparkly star in the night sky and wonders what it is.
story: Jane Taylor wrote the poem The Star, published in 1806 in Rhymes for the Nursery, a book she wrote with her sister Ann. The words were later joined to a French tune first printed in 1761, and appeared together in print by 1838. Only the first of its five verses is widely sung today.
funFact: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Mad Hatter sings a silly version about a twinkling little bat.
myth: Mozart did not write the tune. He composed twelve piano variations on the existing French melody in Vienna around 1781-82.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: French melody 'Ah! vous dirai-je, maman'
aboutKids: A woolly black sheep kindly shares three bags of wool, enough for everyone, even a little boy down the lane.
story: An anonymous rhyme printed around 1744 in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book, with words very close to today's. It is sung to a version of the French tune also used for Twinkle Twinkle Little Star; words and melody were first printed together in 1879.
funFact: In 1951 an early computer in Manchester, England, played it, making it one of the first tunes ever played by a computer.
myth: Often said to protest a medieval wool tax (1275) or to carry a hidden meaning about slavery. The slavery claim has no historical basis, and the tax idea is speculation about a rhyme first printed centuries later.

aboutKids: Friends dance around a bush, then act out their busy day: washing hands, brushing hair, and getting ready.
story: An anonymous circle game. Robert Chambers noted a version in Scotland in 1842, and James Orchard Halliwell recorded it in England in 1849, comparing it to a similar bramble-bush game. Players circle, then mime everyday chores. Its tune is the one Nancy Dawson danced to in The Beggar's Opera in 18th-century London.
funFact: Mulberries actually grow on trees, not bushes, and an older version of the game may have gone around a bramble bush.
myth: Said to have started with women prisoners walking round a mulberry tree at Wakefield Prison. The story comes from one local historian and is unproven.
catalogNote: Catalog cites Halliwell (1840s). An earlier record appears in Robert Chambers's Popular Rhymes of Scotland (1842), as a variant of The Merry-Ma-Tanzie (per Mental Floss; not confirmed in a second source). Halliwell's printing is 1849. Public-domain status is unaffected.

aboutKids: A silly, giggly night: a cat plays the fiddle, a cow jumps over the moon, and a dish runs off with a spoon.
story: An anonymous nonsense rhyme first printed around 1765 in Mother Goose's Melody, though the cat-and-fiddle image is far older; a London inn bore that name by 1587. The Opies called it probably the best-known nonsense verse in English. The usual tune was published by James William Elliott in 1870.
funFact: When people say they are over the moon because they are very happy, they are borrowing a phrase from this rhyme.
myth: Many hidden meanings have been proposed, from historical figures to constellations or the Egyptian goddess Hathor. None is supported; most scholars treat it as pure nonsense verse.

writtenBy: Traditional English nursery rhyme (originally a riddle). Tune: James William Elliott
aboutKids: Humpty Dumpty sits up high on a wall, wobbles, and tumbles down. Even the king's helpers cannot put him back together.
story: This anonymous rhyme was first printed in Samuel Arnold's Juvenile Amusements (1797), with wording different from today's. It probably began as a riddle whose answer was an egg, though the rhyme never says so. Lewis Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass (1871) made Humpty a famous egg character; the usual tune comes from James William Elliott (1870).
funFact: The rhyme never actually says Humpty is an egg. It started as a riddle, and an egg was the answer.
myth: Popularly said to be a cannon on a church wall at the 1648 siege of Colchester, or King Richard III. The cannon story traces to a 1996 tourist website and invented verses; neither theory has evidence.

writtenBy: Traditional American song; familiar tune credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte
aboutKids: We row our little boat gently down a quiet stream, smiling and happy, as if life were a lovely dream.
story: An American song whose words were first printed in 1852 with a different tune. The melody sung today first appeared in The Franklin Square Song Collection (New York, 1881), credited to Eliphalet Oram Lyte, though it is unclear whether he composed or arranged it. It is usually sung as a round.
funFact: It is a round: up to four groups start singing one after another, and the overlapping parts make harmony.
catalogNote: Catalog says the familiar tune was 'published by Lyte'. The 1881 Franklin Square Song Collection was compiled by J. P. McCaskey and credits Lyte, but sources do not say whether Lyte composed or adapted the tune. Public-domain status is unaffected (Lyte died 1913).

writtenBy: Traditional singing game, probably of German origin
aboutKids: A farmer stands in the middle of a circle and picks friends one by one, all the way to a mouse and some cheese.
story: A circle game that probably came from Germany, where a version was recorded in 1826, and was carried to America by immigrants. It was first printed in the US in William Wells Newell's Games and Songs of American Children (1883). Each verse adds a new player to the middle of the ring.
funFact: At the end, the last player chosen, the cheese, stands all by themselves in the middle and often becomes the next farmer.
